intro: Quick semitone clashes give this E-minor étude its crooked smile; the middle opens into an E-major song deep in the piano. Edward Neeman plays the two sides of Chopin’s little scherzo.

sections.label: A · Semitone clashes and clipped chords
sections.mNote: Quick dissonances interrupt the light, scherzando piano writing

sections.label: B · The left hand sings in E major
sections.mNote: A low melody unfolds beneath rising and falling figures

sections.label: A′ · The E-minor joke returns
sections.mNote: Broken rhythms and quick clashes return after the song

sections.label: Coda · E major, fortissimo
sections.mNote: Full chords and an upward flourish end in E major

cues.title: A semitone sideways
cues.text: The right hand keeps brushing against the note next door. These quick semitone clashes give the E-minor tune a teasing edge. Chopin marks the music scherzando — joking — and breaks its phrases into short, lightly played gestures.
cues.evidence: Minor-second dissonances: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._25,_No._5_(Chopin). Vivace, scherzando and broken rhythms: Mieczysław Tomaszewski, https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The left hand sings
cues.text: Più lento: slower, and now in E major. The melody moves down into the left hand, in the range of a cello. Above it, the right hand rises and falls in flowing figures. The little jokes have stopped for a song.
cues.evidence: E-major Più lento: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._25,_No._5_(Chopin). Cello-register melody and accompanying figuration: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A sonata from his teacher
cues.text: Larry Sitsky, one of Neeman’s teachers, writes his First Piano Sonata especially for him. Neeman’s debut album in 2016 places its first recording beside Rachmaninoff.
cues.evidence: Australian National University biography: Sitsky as teacher, the dedicated Sonata No. 1 and Neeman’s March 2016 debut album Rachmaninoff & Sitsky. https://music.cass.anu.edu.au/people/dr-edward-neeman

cues.title: The clipped tune returns
cues.text: The E-minor opening returns at its quicker pace. The low singing line disappears, and the piano resumes its broken rhythms and little dissonant nudges. The hands have traded long phrases for short exchanges.
cues.evidence: Return of the scherzando outer section after the slower trio: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191 and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._25,_No._5_(Chopin).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: E major has the last word
cues.text: The ending suddenly grows emphatic. Fortissimo chords and an upward flourish carry the piano into E major, the key of the middle song. Chopin ends his light scherzo with both hands speaking at full strength.
cues.evidence: Tomaszewski describes the dramatic final turn, fortissimo chords and ascending major-key passage. https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: E major brings a low melody
transitions.from: A · Semitone clashes and clipped chords
transitions.to: B · The left hand sings in E major
transitions.how: The E-minor scherzando closes and Più lento introduces E major. The left hand carries a sustained melody in the cello’s range. Rising and falling right-hand figures replace the opening’s clipped chords and semitone clashes.
transitions.evidence: Slower middle and cello-register melody: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191. Più lento and E major: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._25,_No._5_(Chopin).

transitions.title: E minor brings back the joke
transitions.from: B · The left hand sings in E major
transitions.how: The E-major song closes, and the quick E-minor opening returns. The left hand leaves its long melody; the piano resumes short broken chords and semitone dissonances. The marking scherzando again describes the clipped exchange between the hands.
transitions.evidence: The étude’s scherzo-and-trio design and return: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191 and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Étude_Op._25,_No._5_(Chopin).

transitions.title: The piano ends in E major
transitions.how: The returning E-minor scherzando leads to a forceful coda. Fortissimo chords and an ascending piano flourish establish E major. The major key of the middle song now supplies the closing harmony.
transitions.evidence: Final fortissimo chords and major-key flourish: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/191.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He brought the opera singer’s breath and the mazurka’s wayward accents to a piano that could whisper across a room.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. Chopin had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers; teaching soon supplied his living. He would spend the rest of his life in a profession that depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from triumph to triumph. Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. They moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy already had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
